title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Dining Philosophers problem

N Philosophers sit at a round table with a bowl of rice in the middle
They spend their lives alternating thinking and eating
Between each neighbor is one chopstick
They do not interact with their neighbors
They need two chopsticks to eat
They release the chopsticks when done.
What rules should they follow to avoid deadlock?

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Deadlock

The permanent blocking of a set of processes that either compete for system resources or communicate with each other.
A set of processes is deadlocked when each process in the set is blocked awaiting an event that can only be triggered by another blocked process in the set
In a general case, there is no efficient solution

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
System Model

Systems consist of a finite number of resources
Consider resource types: R1, R2, …, Rm

Could be CPU cycles, memory space, I/O devices, etc

Each resource type Ri has Wi instances
Each process can do each of the following on a resource:

Request: process requests an instance of a resource
Use: process uses the resource
Release: process releases the resource

text:

Data

A semaphore s1 initialized to 1
A semaphore s2 initialized to 1

P1:
semWait(s1)

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Resource Categories

Reusable: Can safely be used by only one process at a time and is not depleted by that use:

Processors, I/O channels, memory, storage, …

Consumable:

A resource that can be created (produced) and destroyed (consumed) by processes:

Messages, signals, data, etc

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Reusable Resource Deadlock

Space is available for allocation of 200 KB, and the following occurs:

P1: … request 80 KB … request 60 KB
P2: … request 70 KB … request 80 KB

Deadlock will occur if both processes are allowed to progress to their second request

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Consumable Resource Deadlock

Consider a pair of processes, in which each process attempts to receive a message from the other process and then send a message to the other process: P1:
...
receive message from P2
...
send message to P2
P2:
...
receive message from P1
...
send message to P1
Deadlock occurs if the Receive is blocking

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Resource Allocation Graph

A directed graph that describes the allocation of resources
A set of vertices V, and edges E
V is partitioned into:

P = {P1, P2, …, Pn} is the set of processes
R = {R1, R2, …, Rm} is the set of resources

E is partitioned into:

Request edge: Pi -> Rj

Pi is requesting an instance of resource Rj

Assignment edge: Rj -> Pi

Rj is assigned to Pi

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Deadlock Characterization

Deadlocks can arise if four conditions are met simultaneously

Mutual Exclusion: Only one process at a time can use a resource
Hold and Wait: A process holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire additional resources held by other processes
No Preemption: A resource can be released only voluntarily by the process holding it, after that process has completed its task
Circular Wait: There exists a set {P0, P1, …, Pn} of waiting processes such that P0 is waiting for a resource held by P1, P1 is waiting for a resource held by P2, …, Pn-1 is waiting for a resource held by Pn, and Pn is waiting for a resource held by P0

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Some Basic Facts

If a graph contains no cycles, then no deadlock can occur
If a graph contains a cycle:

If only one instance per resource type, then deadlock
If several instances per resource type, possibility of deadlock

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Methods for Handling Deadlocks

There is no single effective strategy that can deal with all deadlock types
There are three common approaches:

Deadlock prevention:

Disallow one of the three necessary conditions for deadlock occurrence, or prevent circular wait condition from happening

Deadlock detection:

Grant resource requests, when possible, but periodically check for the presence of deadlocks and take action to recover

Deadlock Avoidance:

Do not grant a resource request if this allocation may lead to a deadlock

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Deadlock Prevention Strategy

Design a system in such a way that the possibility of deadlock is excluded
Two methods:

Indirect:

Prevent the occurrence of one of the three necessary conditions

Direct:

Prevent the occurrence of circular wait condition

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Deadlock Condition Prevention

Mutual Exclusion:

CANNOT be disallowed in general
If access to a resource requires mutual exclusion, then mutual exclusion must be supported by the OS
Some resources, such as files, may allow multiple accesses for reads but only exclusive access for writes
Even in this case, deadlock can occur if more than one process requires write permission

Hold and Wait:

Require that a process request all of its required resources at one time and blocking the process until all requests can be granted simultaneously
This is not practical, as it is quite inefficient

No Preemption:

If a process holding certain resources is denied a further request, that process must release its original resources and request them again
OS may preempt the second process and require it to release its resources

Circular Wait:

The circular wait condition can be prevented by defining a linear ordering of resource types

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Deadlock Avoidance

Allows the three necessary conditions but makes judicious choices to assure that the deadlock point is never reached
A decision is made dynamically whether the current resource allocation request will, if granted, potentially lead to a deadlock
Requires knowledge of future process requests

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Resource Allocation Denial

Referred to as the banker’s algorithm
Definitions:

State of the system reflects the current allocation of resources to processes
Safe state: The system can allocate resources to each thread (up to its maximum) in some order and still avoid deadlock (there is at least one sequence of resource allocations to processes that does not result in a deadlock)
Unsafe state: A state that is not safe (may lead to deadlock)

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Facts

If a system is in a safe state, there is no deadlock
If a system is in an unsafe state, there may be a deadlock
Avoidance ensures that a system will never enter an unsafe state

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Banker’s Algorithm

Multiple instances of resources
Each process must have a priori claim maximum use
When a process requests a resource, it may have to wait
When a process gets all its resources, it must return them in a finite amount of time

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
section: Data Structures for the Banker’s Algorithm
text:
Data Structures for the Banker’s Algorithm

Let n = number of processes and m = number of resource types
Available: A vector of length m. If Available[j] = k, then there are k instances of resource type Rj available
Max: An n x m matrix. If Max[i,j] = k, then process Pi may request at most k instances of resource type Rj
Allocation: An n x m matrix. If Allocation[i,j] = k, then Pi is currently allocated k instances of resource type Rj
Need: An n x m matrix. If Need[i,j] = k, then Pi may need k more instances of resource type Rj to complete its task

Need[i,j] = Max[i,j] - Allocation[i,j]

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Deadlock Avoidance Restrictions

Maximum resource requirements for each process must be stated in advance
Processes under consideration must be independent and with no synchronization requirements
There must be a fixed number of resources to allocate
No process may be terminated while holding resources

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Deadlock Detection

Allows the system to enter a deadlock state
Detection algorithm:

A check for deadlock can be made as frequently as each resource request, or less frequently, depending on how likely it is for a deadlock to occur
The algorithm is relatively simple
For a single instance of each resource type: maintain a wait-for graph (nodes are processes; Pi -> Pj if Pi is waiting for Pj). Periodically search for a cycle — O(n^2)
For multiple instances per resource type: use Available, Allocation, and Request matrices (similar to banker’s)

Recovery scheme

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Recovery from Deadlock

Process Termination:

Abort all deadlocked processes (simple but costly)
Abort one process at a time until the deadlock cycle is eliminated
Order to abort based on: priority, how long the process has computed, resources used, resources still needed, number of processes that would need to be terminated, whether interactive or batch

Resource Preemption:

Selecting a victim: minimize cost
Rollback: return to a safe state and restart the process from that state
Starvation risk: the same process may always be selected as victim; include number of rollbacks in cost factor to prevent this

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Integrated Deadlock Strategy

Rather than using a single strategy for all deadlock types, it can be more efficient to group resources into classes and apply the most appropriate strategy per class
Classes of resources and their typical strategies:

Swappable space (secondary storage for swapping): Prevention via hold-and-wait (allocate all required resources at once)
Process resources (devices, files): Avoidance is often effective since processes can declare resource needs in advance
Main memory: Prevention by preemption (swap preempted process to secondary memory)
Internal resources (I/O channels): Prevention via resource ordering

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Types of Scheduling

Long-term Scheduling: The decision to add to the pool of processes to be run
Medium-term Scheduling: The decision to add to the number of processes that are partially or fully in memory
Short-term Scheduling: The decision as to which available processes will be executed by the processor
I/O Scheduling: The decision as to which process’s pending I/O request shall be handled by an available I/O device

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
The Main goal of Scheduling

Aim to assign processes to be executed by the processor in a way that meets system objectives such as response time, throughput, and processor efficiency

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Scheduling Criteria: User Oriented

Performance related

Turnaround Time: The interval of time between process creation and its completion. Includes actual execution time, plus time spent waiting for resources, including the processor. This is generally used for batch jobs.
Response Time: For an interactive process, this is the time from the submission of a request until the response begins to be received. Often a process can begin to produce some output to the user while continuing to process the request. Thus, this is a better measure than turnaround time from a User’s point of view. This is generally for time sensitive / real-time systems such as websites
Deadlines: When process completion deadlines can be specified, the scheduling discipline should subordinate other goals to that of maximizing the percentage of deadlines met

Other

Predictability: A given job should run in about the same amount of time and at about the same cost, regardless of the load on the system

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Scheduling Criteria: System Oriented

Performance related:

Throughput: The scheudling policy should attempt to maximize the number of processes completed per unit of time. This is a measure of how much work is being performed. This clearly depends on the average amount of time a process takes, but is also influenced by the scheudling policy used.
Processor Utilization: This is the percentage of time that the processor is busy. For expensive shared systems, this is a significant criterion. In single user systems, and some other systems (such as real time), this criteria is less important than others

Other:

Fairness: In absence of guidance from the user, or other system supplied guidance, processes should be treated the same, and no process should suffer starvation (lack of resources).
Priority Enforcement: When processes are assigned priorities, the scheudling policy should favor high priority processes.
Resource Balancing: The scheduling policy should keep the resources of the system busy. Processes that will underutilize stressed resources should be favored. This criteria mostly refers to long and medium term scheudling

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Long Term Scheduler

Determines what programs are admitted to the system for processing
Controls the degree of multiprogramming

The more processes that are created, the smaller the percentage of time that each process can be executed
May be limited to provide satisfactory services to the current set of processes

Creates processes from a queue when it can, but must decide:

When the OS can take on one or more additional processes
Which jobs to accept and turn into processes

Can be first come, first served
Can be dictated by priority, expected execution time, I/O requirements

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Medium Term Scheduler

Part of Admit and Swapping functions
Swapping decisions are based on need for resources and to manage the degree of multiprogramming

Considers the resources needed of the swapped out (suspended) process

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Short Term Scheduler

Known as the dispatcher
Executes the most frequently
Makes the fine-grained decision of which process to execute next
Invoked when an even occurs that may lead to the blocking of the current process, or that may provide an opportunity to preempt a currently running process in favor of another

Examples:

clock interrupts
I/O interrupts
OS system calls
Signals (i.e. Semaphores (discussed later))

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Short Term Scheduler Criteria

Performance:

Quantitative
Easily measured
Throughput/Response time

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Process Behavior

Processes alternate bursts of computing with I/O requests

Some processes spend most of their time computing: CPU bound
Some processes spend most of their time waiting for I/O: I/O bound

There are generally more small-medium cpu bursts than long

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
CPU Scheduler

The CPU scheduler selects from among processes in the ready queue and allocates a CPU core (uniprocessor) to one of them

Queue can be ordered by burst time, priority, execution time, etc.

CPU Scheduler can make 4 choices based on process states:

Switch from running to waiting
Switch from running to ready
Switch from waiting to ready
Terminate the process

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Selection Function

Determines which process, among ready processes, is selected for next execution
May be based on priority, resource management, or execution charactaristcs of the process

If based on charactaristcs, the important quanitites are:

w: Time spent waiting in the system
e: Time spent in execution
s: Total serivce time required by the process, including e: generally this quantity must be estimated or supplied by the user

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Preemptive Scheduling and Nonpreemptive Scheduling

Nonpreemptive scheduling: Once the CPU has been allocated to a process, the process keeps the CPU until it either releases by switching to waiting, or is terminated
Anything else is preemptive
Virtually all modern OS (like windows, mac, etc) use preemptive scheduling

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Preemptive Scheduling and Race conditions

Preemptive scheduling can result in race conditions when data is shared between several processes
Consider a case where two processes share the same data. While one process is updating the data, it is preempted so that the second process can run. The second process then tries to read the data, but it is in an inconsistent state. ← Race condition

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Dispatcher Latency

Dispatcher latency: The time it takes for the dispatcher to stop one process from running and start running another process

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Scheduling Algorithms

First-Come, First-Served (FCFS):

The simplest CPU-Scheduling Algorithm
Processes are assigned to the CPU in the order they arrive in the ready queue
Nonpreemptive algorithm: Once a process is in the running state, it continues until it is blocked or terminated
Average W: W = (T1 + T2 + T3 + … Tn) / n
Convoy effect: Short processes behind long processes have a higher average wait time

Shortest Job First (SJF):

Associate each process with length of its next CPU burst

Use these lengths to schedule the process with the shortest time

SJF is optimal for nonpreemptive methods: gives minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes
How do we determine the length of the next CPU burst?

Ask the user
estimate
This is why this method is hard to implement

Preemptive version of the algorithm is Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)

Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF):

Like SJF, but if a shorter job arrives, the current job is preempted

Round Robin (RR):

Preemptive
Each process gets a small unit of CPU time (time quantum q), usually 10-100 ms. After this time has elapsed the process is preempted and added to the end of the ready queue.
If there are n processes in the ready queue and the time quantum is q, then each process gets 1/n of the CPU time in chunks of at most q time units at once. No process waits more than (n-1)q time units.
Timer interrupts every q to dispatch next process
Large q: Becomes much like FCFS
Small q: dispatcher latency increases and decreases efficiency

Priority Scheduling:

A priority number (integer) is associated with each process
The CPU is allocated to the process(es) with the highest priority (the smaller int is higher priority)

Preemptive or Nonpreemptive

SRTF is used if multiple processes of the same priority arrive and it is preemptive
SJF is used for multiple processes of the same priorirty and it is non preemptive
Problem: Starvation - Low priority processes may never execute

Solution: Aging - As time progresses, increase the priority of a process

Multilevel queues:

With priority scheduling, we have a seperate queue for each priority
Schedule each process from its related priority queue

Prioritization based on process type:

Highest priority: Real-time processes
System processes
Interactive processes
Lowest priority: Batch processes

Objectives

title: 06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
text:
Background

OS design is concerned with management of process and threads:

Multiprogramming:

The management of multiple processes within a uniprocessor system

Multiprocessing:

The management of multiple processes within a multiprocessor system

Distributed processing:

The management of multiple processes executing on multiple, distributed computer systems


Processes can execute concurrently

May be interrupted at any time, partially completing execution

Concurrent access to shared data may result in data inconsistency
Maintaining data consistency requires mechanisms to ensure the orderly execution of cooperating processes

title: 06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
text:
Race Conditions

Occurs when multiple processes or threads read and write the same data items
The final result depends on the order of execution

The “loser” of the race is the process that updates last and will determine the final value of variables

Ex:

Process p0 and p1 are creating child processes using the fork() system call
Race condition on kernel variable next_available_pid which represents the next available process ID
Unless there is a mechanism to prevent p0 and p1 from accessing the variable next_available_pid at the same time, the same PID could be assigned to two different processes

title: 06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
text:
Terms related to concurrency

Atomic Operations: A function or action implemented as a sequence of one or more instructions that appear to be indivisible; that is, no other process can see an intermediate state or be interrupt that operation. The sequence of instructions is guaranteed to execute as a group, or not execute at all, having no visible effect on system state. Atomicity guarantees isolation from concurrent processes.
Critical Section: A section of code within a process that requires access to shared resources and that must not be executed while another process is in a corresponding section of code.
Deadlock: A situation in which two or more processes are unable to proceed because each is waiting for the other to do something
Livelock: A situation in which two or more processes continuously change their state in response to changes in another process without doing any useful work.

Ex: Two processes are attempting to acquire the same lock and continuously release and reacquire the lock without making progress

Mutual Exclusion: The requirement that when one process is in a critical section that accesses shared resources, no other process may be in a critical section that accesses any of the same resources
Starvation: A situation in which a runnable process is overlooked indefinitely by the scheduler, although it is ready to proceed, it is never selected.

title: 06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
text:
The Critical Section Problem

Consider n processes in a system {p0, p1, p2, … pn-1}
Each process has a critical section (CS) segment of code

The processes may be changing common variables, updating tables, writing files, etc.
When one process is in CS, no other process may be in its CS

CS problem: Design a protocol to solve the issues above
General Structure for a process pi:

while(1){
[entry section]
critical section
[exit section]
remainder section
}

Requirements:

Mutual Exclusion: If process Pi is executing its critical section, then no other processes can be executing their CS
Progress: If no process is executing its CS, and there exists some process that wishes to enter their CS, then the selection of the process that will enter the CS cannot be postponed indefinitely
Bounded Waiting: A bound must exist on the number of times that other processes are allowed to enter their CS after a process has made a request to enter its CS and before that request is granted

Assume that each process executes at a nonzero speed
No assumption concerning relative speeds of the n processes

title: 06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
section: Software Solutions to the Critical Section Problem

title: 06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
text:
Peterson’s Solution and Modern Architecture

Although useful for demonstrating an algorithm, Peterson’s solution is not guaranteed to work on modern architectures
To improve performance, processors and/or compilers may reorder operations that have no dependencies
For single-threaded programs this is fine; for multithreaded programs the ordering may produce inconsistent or unexpected results
Example:

Two threads share: bool flag = false; int x = 0;
Thread 1: while (!flag); print x
Thread 2: x = 100; flag = true
Expected output: 100
However, Thread 2’s instructions may be reordered to: flag = true; x = 100
This could cause Thread 1 to print 0 — a race condition

title: 06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
text:
Memory Barriers

Memory models are the memory guarantees a computer architecture makes to application programs

Strongly ordered: A memory modification of one processor is immediately visible to all other processors
Weakly ordered: A memory modification of one processor may not be immediately visible to all other processors

A memory barrier is an instruction that forces any change in memory to be propagated (made visible) to all other processors
When a memory barrier instruction is performed, the system ensures that all loads and stores are completed before any subsequent load or store operations are performed
Memory Barrier Example (fixing the Peterson’s reordering issue):

Thread 1: while (!flag); memory_barrier(); print x
Thread 2: x = 100; memory_barrier(); flag = true
Thread 1 is guaranteed that flag is loaded before x
Thread 2 ensures the assignment to x occurs before the assignment to flag

title: 06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
text:
Synchronization Hardware

Many systems provide hardware support for implementing the critical section code
Uniprocessors: could disable interrupts (generally too inefficient on multiprocessor systems)
Two key hardware instructions:

Test-and-Set
Compare-and-Swap

Test-and-Set instruction:

Executed atomically
Returns the original value of the passed parameter
Sets the new value of the passed parameter to true
Solution: Shared Boolean variable lock, initialized to false

while (test_and_set(&lock));  /* busy wait */
/* critical section */
lock = false;
/* remainder section */
Compare-and-Swap instruction:

Executed atomically
Returns the original value of the passed parameter value
Sets the variable value to new_value, but only if *value == expected (the swap takes place only under this condition)
Solution: Shared integer lock initialized to 0

while (compare_and_swap(&lock, 0, 1) != 0);  /* busy wait */
/* critical section */
lock = 0;
/* remainder section */

title: 06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
text:
Mutex Locks

Boolean variable indicating if the lock is available or not
Protect a critical section by:

First acquiring the lock: acquire()
Then releasing the lock: release()

Calls to acquire() and release() must be atomic
Usually implemented via hardware atomic instructions such as compare-and-swap
This solution requires busy waiting — referred to as a spinlock
Solution to the CS Problem Using Mutex Locks:
while (true) {
  acquire lock
  critical section
  release lock
  remainder section
}

title: 06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
text:
Semaphores

A semaphore may be initialized to a nonnegative integer value
The semWait operation decrements the semaphore value
The semSignal operation increments the semaphore value
Implementation must be atomic (can be implemented in hardware or software)

Software schemes such as Dekker’s or Peterson’s algorithms can be used
Hardware-supported mutual exclusion schemes are another alternative

Binary Semaphore: Value is restricted to 0 or 1 (essentially a mutex lock)
Counting Semaphore: Value can range over an unrestricted domain
Strong vs. Weak Semaphores:

A queue is used to hold processes waiting on the semaphore
Strong semaphore: Processes are released from the queue in FIFO order
Weak semaphore: No specific order for release is specified

title: 04 · Multiprocessor Scheduling
text:
Classifications of Multiprocessor Systems:

Loosely Coupled/Distributed Microprocessors or cluster processors:

Consists of a collection of relatively autonomous systems, each processor having its own main memory and I/O channels

Functionally specialized processor:

There is a primary, general-purpose processor
Specialized processors are generally controlled by the primary processor, and provide services to it

Tightly Coupled Multiprocessors:

Consists of a set of processors that share common main memory and are under the integrated control of the OS
Symmetrical MultiProcessing (SMP) is the most common modern example of this


Synchronization granularity in processes








Grain Size
Description
Sync Interval (instructions)




Fine
Parallelism inherent in a single instruction stream
< 20


Medium
Parallel processing or multitasking within a single application
20 – 200


Coarse
Multiprocessing of concurrent processes in a multiprogrammed env.
200 – 2,000


Very Coarse
Distributed processes across network nodes
2,000 – 1M


Independent
Multiple unrelated processes
N/A



Independent Parallelism

No explicit synchronization between processes

Each process represents a separate, independent job or application
Typically used in time-sharing systems where each user is (generally) performing an independent job

Multiprocessor provides the same service as a multiprogrammed uniprocessor
Because there are multiple processors, average user response time is lower

Coarse/Very Coarse:

There is synchronization between processes, but at a very low level
Easily handled as a set of concurrent processes running on a multiprogrammed processor
Can be supported on a multiprocessor with little to no change in user software

Medium-Grained Parallelism

Single application can be effectively implemented as a collection of threads within a single process

Programmer must explicitly specify the potential parallelism in code
There needs to be a high-degree of coordination and interaction among threads of an application

Because the various threads of an application interact so frequently, scheduling decisions concerning one thread may affect the performance of the entire application

Think of if a single thread gets blocked, and the others don’t wait, which could cause data inconsistency


Fine-Grained Parallelism

Represents a much more complex use of parallelism than is found in the use of threads in code
Mostly OS/Scheduler, or hardware based

Design issues:

The approach taken to scheduling depends on a couple of things:

The granularity of applications
Speed of applications
The number of processors you have available

Scheduling on a multiprocessor involves three interrelated issues:

The dispatching of a process (separate but linked to the assignment of a process)
Assignment of processes to processors
Use of multiprogramming on an individual proccesor/core


Assignment of processes to a processor:

Assuming all processors are equal, it is simplest to treat processors like a pooled resource and assign processes to processors as needed

Dynamic Assignment

If a process is permanently assigned to a processor from activation to termination

Static Assignment
Each processor has its own short term assignment queue
The advantage is that there may be less overhead in the scheduling function
Allows for group/gang scheduling
Disadvantage:

Load imbalance: One processor could be idle, with an empty queue, while another processor has a backlog
The simplest solution is to provide a common queue of processes shared across all processors, or use dynamic load balancing



There are two methods of process assignment to a processor used for both static and dynamic methods:

Primary/Secondary Architecture
Peer Assignment

Primary Secondary Architecture

Primary processor executes key kernel functions, and schedules for all other processors
Secondary processors provides services for the primary
Think of the primary as the brain, and secondary as arms or legs
Advantages:

Simple, and requires very little enhancement to a multiprogrammed uniprocessor system
Conflict resolution for resources and synchronization is simplified since one processor has control

Disadvantage:

Single point of failure: If the primary fails, the system fails
Primary can become a performance bottleneck: If a lot of small processes are sent to schedule at the same time, it would take longer to distribute each task to a processor than it would take for that processor to complete that task


Peer Architecture:

Kernel can execute on any processor
Each processor does self-scheduling from a pool of available processes

In traditional multicore systems, processes are not dedicated to a single processor. Dynamic Assignment is most common.
A single process queue is used for all processors to retrieve tasks from

If some priority scheme is used, there are multiple queues, one for each priority


Thread Scheduling:

Thread execution is separated from the rest of a process
An application can be a set of threads that cooperate and execute concurrently (or in parallel) in the same memory address space
On a uniprocessor (concurrent system), threads can be used as a program structuring aid, and allows overlap of I/O processing
In a multiprocessor system, threads can be used to exploit true parallelism of an application

Dramatic gains in performance are possible in multiprocessor system due to this

Four approaches to thread scheduling:

Load sharing: Threads are not assigned to a particular processor
Gang Scheduling: A set of related threads are scheduled to run on a set of processors at the same time on a one-to-one basis
Dedicated Processor Assignment: Provides implicit scheduling defined by the assignment of threads to processors
Dynamic Scheduling: The number of threads in a process can be altered during the course of execution


Load Sharing:

Simplest approach and the one that carries over the most from uniprocessor environments
Advantages:

Load is distributed evenly across all processors, ensuring that no processor is idle while there is work available to do
No centralized scheduler required
There is a global queue of threads that is easier to organize and access

Disadvantages:

Central queue occupies a region of memory that must be accessed in a manner that enforces mutual exclusion (so multiple processors can’t take the same process)

Leads to performance bottleneck

Preemptive threads are unlikely to resume execution on the same processor

Caching becomes less efficient, leading to another performance bottleneck

If all threads are treated as a common pool of threads, it is unlikely that all of the threads of a program will gain access to processors at the same time

Decreases efficiency of parallel processes
The process switches could seriously compromise performance


Common implementations of Load sharing:

FCFS
Smallest number of threads first
Preemptive smallest number of threads first


Gang/Group Scheduling:

A set of related threads is scheduled to run on a set of processors at the same time on a one-to-one basis
Can be uniform or weighted:

Uniform: As processes have no weight, all the threads in one process will execute before the threads of another process, alternating until completion
Weighted: Processes are prioritized such that all of the threads of a higher priority process will execute until completion before another process executes

Advantages:

Synchronization and blocking may be reduced, as there is less process switching
Scheduling process overhead may be reduced
Useful for medium/fine grained applications whose performance severely degrades when any part of the application is not running, while other parts are ready to run

Disadvantage:

If there is a large process queue, a process will likely take longer to execute while waiting for processors to be freed for each of its threads


Dedicated processor assignment:

When an application is scheduled, each of its threads is assigned to a processor that remains dedicated to that thread until the application is completed
If a thread of an application is blocked waiting for I/O or for synchronization with another thread then that thread’s processor remains idle
Defense of this strategy:

In a highly parallel system with tens or hundreds of processors, processor utilization is no longer an important metric of a system
The total avoidance of process switching during the lifetime of a process should result in a substantial speedup of that process

title: 04 · Multiprocessor Scheduling
text:
Dynamic Scheduling

This method allows an application to adjust the number of threads used during execution
This allows the OS to adjust the load on processors to improve utilization by reallocating resources based on current workload
When a job requests one or more processors (either when the job arrives for the first time, or because its requirements change):

If there are idle processors, use them to satisfy the request
If there are no idle processors, and if the job making the request is a new arrival:

allocate a single processor by taking one away from any current job that currently holds more than one processor

If any portion of the request cannot be satisfied (if all current processes only have a single processor), the new job remains outstanding until either a processor becomes available, or the job is rescinded

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
The Security Problem

System is secure if resources are used and accessed as intended under all circumstances.

This is basically impossible to achieve.

Some terms:

Intruder/Attacker: Someone attempting to breach security
Threat: A potential security violation (suspected but not always verified)
Attack: An attempt to breach security

Can be accidental or malicious

Vulnerability: A weakness in the system that can be exploited
Easier to protect against accidental attacks than malicious ones

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Security Violation Categories

Breach of confidentiality: Unauthorized access to sensitive data
Breach of integrity: Unauthorized modification of data
Breach of availability: Unauthorized destruction of data
Theft of service: Unauthorized use of system resources
Denial of service (DOS): Prevention of legitimate use

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
System Access Threats

System access threats fall into two general categories:

Intruders: Individuals who attempt to gain unauthorized access to a system
Malicious software: Programs that attempt to exploit system vulnerabilities

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Intruder Types

Masquerader: An individual who is not authorized to use the computer and who penetrates a system’s access controls to exploit a legitimate user’s account

Example: A hacker who steals a password to gain access to a system

Misfeasor: A legitimate user who accesses data, programs, or resources for which such access is not authorized, or who is authorized for such access, but misuses their privileges

Example: An employee who accesses sensitive data for personal gain

Clandestine user: An individual who seizes supervisory control of the system and uses this control to evade auditing and access controls or to suppress audit collection

Example: A hacker who gains root access to a system and disables auditing features

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Security Violation Methods

Masquerading (breach authentication):

Pretending to be an authorized user to escalate privileges

Replay attack:

As is or with message modification

Man-in-the-middle attack, now normally called a On-Path attack:

Intruder sits in data flow, masquerading as sender to receiver and vice versa

Session hijacking:

Intercept an already established session to bypass authentication

Privilege escalation:

Common attack with access beyond what a user or resource is supposed to have

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Malicious Software

Programs that exploit vulnerabilities in a computer system
Also called malware
Can be split into two categories:

Parasitic: Fragments of programs that cannot exist independently of some real application program, utility, or system program

Viruses, logic bombs, and backdoors are examples

Independent: Self contained programs that can be scheduled and run by the operating system

Worms and bot programs are examples


There are a multitude of different types of malware, with many names
Trojan horse:

Code segment that misuses its environment
Exploits mechanisms for allowing programs written by users to be executed by other users
Spyware, popup browser windows, covert channels
Up to 80% of spam delivered by spyware-infected systems

Trap Door:

Specific user identifier or password that circumvents normal security procedures
Could be included in a compiler

Malware:

Software designed to exploit, disable, or damage computers
Spyware: Programs frequently installed with legitimate software to display ads and capture user data
Ransomware: Locks up data via encryption and demands payment for decryption key

Others include trap doors, logic bombs
All try to violate the principle of least privilege
Goal frequently is to leave behind a Remote Access Tool (RAT) for repeated access

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Principle of Least Privilege

A user should be given the minimum levels of access necessary to perform his/her job functions
This is a fundamental principle of computer security
Is used to limit the potential damage that can be done by a compromised account or system
“The purpose of this principle is to reduce the number of potential interactions among privileged programs to the minimum necessary to operate correctly, so that one may develop confidence that unintentional, unwanted, or improper uses of privilege do not occur”

Jerome H. Saltzer describing a design principle for the Multics operating system in ’74

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Four Layer Model of Security

The four layers of security are:

Physical security

Attacks: console access, hardware-based attacks
Countermeasures: locks, guards, vaults, device data encryption

Network security

Attacks: sniffing, spoofing, masquerading
Countermeasures: encryption, authentication, filtering

Operating system security

Attacks: insecure defaults, platform vulnerabilities
Countermeasures: patches, reconfiguration, hardening

Application security

Attacks: logic bugs, design flaws, code injection
Countermeasures: sandboxing, software restrictions

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Countermeasures

RFC 4949: Internet Security Glossary

Defines intrusion detection as a security service that monitors and analyzes system events for the purpose of finding, and providing real-time or near real-time alerts of, attempts to access system resources in an unauthorized manner
Intrusion detection systems (IDS) can be classified as:

Host-based IDS (HIDS): Monitors a single host for suspicious activity
Network-based IDS (NIDS): Monitors network traffic for suspicious activity for a network segment.

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
IDS components

Sensors

Responsible for collecting data
The input for a sensor may be any part of a system that could contain evidence of an intrusion
Types of input to a sensor include network packets, log files, and system call traces

Analyzers

Receive input from sensors or other analyzers
Responsible for determining if an intrusion has occurred
Must provide guidance about what actions to take as a result of the intrusion

User interface (UI)

Enables a user to view output from the system or control the behavior of the system
May equate to the manager, director, or console component

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
User Authentication

In most computer security contexts, user authentication is the fundamental building block and the primary line of defense
RFC 4949 defines user authentication as the process of verifying an identity claimed by or for a system entity
An authentication process consists of two steps:

Identification: The entity presents an identifier to the system
Verification: Presenting or generating authentication information that corroborate the binding between the entity and the identifier

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Means of Authentication

Something you know: Passwords, PINs, answers to security questions
Something you have: Smart cards, tokens, key fobs
Something you are: Biometrics (fingerprints, retina scans)
Something you do: Behavioral biometrics (typing patterns, mouse movements)
Somewhere you are: Geolocation data (IP address, GPS coordinates)
Something that is in the user’s environment: Surroundings/ambient sounds or ambient access points

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Access control

Implements a security policy that specifies who or what may have access to each specific system resource, and the type of access that is permitted in each instance
Mediates between a user and system resources, such as applications, operating systems, firewalls, routers, files, and databases
A security administrator maintains an authorization database that specifies what type of access to which resources is allowed for this user

The access control function consults this database to determine whether to grant access

An auditing function monitors and keeps record of user accesses to system resources

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Cryptography as a Security Tool

Means to constrain potential senders (sources) and/or receivers (destinations) of messages

Based on secret informations (keys)
Enables:

Confirmation of source
Receipt only by certain destinations
Trust relationship between sender and receiver


Note: symmetric cryptography based on transformation, asymmetric is based on mathematical functions

Asymmetric is much more compute intensive
Typically not used for bulk data encryption

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Buffer Overflow

When more input is placed into a buffer than its capacity allows, which can overwrite other information and be exploited by attackers to crash systems or insert malicious code (more common) to gain control of the system

Also known as buffer overrun

Stack overflow:

A classic attack
A type of buffer overflow that occurs in the call stack of a program
Can occur when a program uses too much stack space, causing the stack to overflow into adjacent memory areas

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Defense against Buffer Overflow

Compile-time:

Programming language
Safe Coding techniques
use of safe libraries
Stack protection

Stack canaries


Runtime:

Executable address space protection
Address space layout randomization (ASLR)
Guard pages

title: 03 · Threads
text:
PCB vs Process Image:

PCB: Data Structure maintained by the OS for every process

Contains essential information about the process such as process state, program counter, register info, memory management info, accounting info, I/O status, and CPU scheduling

Process Image:

The entire collection of information that makes up what is being executed by a process

Includes code, data, and the process stack



Multiprogramming:

When multiprogramming is used, CPU utilization can be improved

If the average process computes only 30% of the time it is sitting in memory, then we can have three processes in memory at once, and the CPU should be busy all of the time.
This is unrealistic at best, however, since it assumes that all processes will never be waiting for I/O at the same time

It is better to view multiprogramming from a probabilistic standpoint.

Suppose that a process spends a fraction of its time (p) waiting for I/O
With multiple processes in memory at once, the probability that all processes are waiting for I/O is p ^ n (n is number of processes)
CPU Utilization = 1 - p^n

Suppose that a computer has 8 GB of memory, with the OS and its tables taking up 2 GB, and each process also taking 2 GB, what is the CPU utilization with 80% chance a process is waiting? .488

What is the new CPU utilization if 8GB of memory are added? .79
What is the new utilization if another 8GB are added? .914

title: 03 · Threads
text:
Threads

Charactaristics of processes:

Resource Ownership:

Processes include virtual memory space to hold a process image
The OS performs a protection function to prevent unwanted interference between processes with respect to resources

Scheduling/Execution:

Follows an execution path that may be interleaed with other processes (multiprogramming)
A process has an execution state and a dispatch priority, and is the entity that is scheduled and dispatched by the OS.


A process is a whole

The unit of resource ownership

A thread is a lightweight part of the process

The unit of dispatching of a process is called a thread, or lightweight process

Multithreading: The ability of an OS to support multiple concurrent paths of execution in a single process

All threads in a multithreaded process with share code, data, and files from a process, but have their own (smaller) registers, stack, and program counter

Single Thread Approach: A single thread of execution per process, in which the concept of a thread is not recognized.

Example: MS-DOS

The process in a multithreaded environment is defined as “the unit of resource allocation and unit of protection”

Things associated with the process:

the virtual address space that holds the process image
protected access to resources

processors
files
I/O resources

Things associated with the thread:

An execution state
Saved thread context
An execution stack
Some per-thread static storage for local variables (register set)
Access to the memory and resources of its process, shared with all threads of that process


Benefits of using threads:

Takes less time to create and terminate
Switching between two threads takes less time than switching between processes
Threads enhance efficiency of interprocess communication

title: 03 · Threads
text:
Multicore Programming

Multicore processessing is the ability for multiple cores on a CPU to execute a process (or threads)
Provides opportunity to increase efficiency, but comes with some drawbacks:

Dividing activites between cores
Balancing work between cores
Dividing data
Data dependency
Testing and debugging

Two types of multicore programming

Parallel processing: implies a system can perform more than one task simultaneously
Concurrent processing: More than one task makes progress at a time in a single core or single core processor, allowed by the scheduler

title: 03 · Threads
text:
Back to Threads

Scheduling: In an OS that supports Threads, scheduling and dispatching is done on a thread by thread basis as opposed to a process by process basis

Most state information dealing with execution is maintained in thread level data structures instead of process level data structures; however:

Suspending a process involves suspending all the threads involved
Termination of a process terminates all threads in a process


Thread execution states:

Process level states: Ready, Blocked, Suspended, Running, Terminated, New
Threads level states: Running, Ready, Blocked
Thread operations associated with a change of states: Spawn, Block, Unblock, Finish

Thread Synchronization

It is necessary to synchronize the activities of the various threads

All threads of a process share the same address space and resources
Any alteration of a resource by one thread affects other threads in the same process, so timing it of significant importance

title: 03 · Threads
text:
Types of Threads

User Level Threads (ULTs)

All thread management is done by the application
The kernel is not aware of the existence of threads

Advantages of ULTs:

Thread switching does not require kernel mode privileges
Scheduling is application specific
ULTs can run on any OS.

Disadvantages of ULTs:

In a typical OS, many system calls are blocking (have to wait for an event). As a result, when a ULT executes a system call, not only is that thread blocked, but all of the threads within that process are blocked as well.
In a pure ULT strategy, a multithreaded application cannot take advantage of multiprocessing. A kernel only assigns one process to a single processor at a time, therefore only a single thread within a process can execute at a time.

Overcoming ULT Disadvantages:

Jacketing: Convert blocking system calls into non-blocking system calls
Writing an application as multiple processes (so they can use multiple processors) rather than multiple threads, though this does eliminate the core advantage of threads



Kernel Level Threads (KLTs)

Thread management is does by the kernel
There is no thread management code in the application level, but an application programming interface (API) is used to interact with the kernel thread facility

Windows is an OS that uses the KLT approach

Advantages of the KLT approach:

The kernel can simultaneously schedule multiple threads from the same process across multiple cores
If one thread of a process is blocked, the kernel can schedule another thread from the same process
Kernel routines themselves can be multithreaded

Disadvantage of the KLT approach:

The transfer of control from one thread to anther within the same process requires a mode switch (similar to a context switch), which when overperformed can cause a system to become inefficient


Combined approach: Thread creation is done completely in the user space, as is the bulk of scheduling and synchronization of threads within an application, while the kernel space is used for processor/core assignment
Thread Libraries

Thread libraries provide a programmer with an API for creating and managing threads
Ways of implementation:

Libraries entirely in user space (pthreads)
Kernel-level libraries supported by the OS

Pthreads:

Stored in user space, interfaces with the kernel
A POSIX standard (IEEE 1003.1c) API for thread creation and synchronization
Common in UNIX OS

pthread_create: fuction used to create a thread

int pthread_create(pthread_t tid, pthread_attr_t attr, func f, void arg);

returns 0 if everything works, nonzero on error


pthread_exit: Terminates a thread

void pthread_exit(void *thread_return)

pthread_join: Main thread waits for another thread to terminate

int pthread_join(pthread_t tid, void **thread_return)

pthread_yield: Release the CPU and allows another thread to run
pthread_attr_init: create and initialize a thread’s attribute structure
pthread_attr_destroy: remove a thread’s attribute structure

Fork-Join Parallelism: Multiple threads (tasks/jobs) are forked, execute individually, and join back up

General Algorithm for fork-join strategy:
if problem is small enough:
    solve the problem directly

else: (problem is large or can be broken down)
    subtask1 = fork(new Task(subset of problem))
    subtask2 = fork(new Task(subset of problem))

    result1 = join(subtask1)
    result2 = join(subtask2)

    return result1 combined with result2

title: 03 · Threads
text:
Threading Issues (in programming)

The semantics of fork() and exec() can change in a multithreaded program:

Does fork() duplicate only the calling thread or all threads?

Linux (POSIX): Child process is created with a single thread
Solaris: Either single threaded child or duplication of all threads is allowed

Exec works as normal, replace the running process with the called process, including all threads

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Relocation

Programmers typically do not know in advance which other programs will be resident in main memory at the time of execution of their program
Active processes need to be able to be swapped in and out of main memory in order to maximize processor utilization
Specifying that a process must be placed in the same memory region when it is swapped back in would be limiting

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Protection

Need to ensure that a process can access only those addresses in its address space
We can provide this protection by using a pair of base and limit registers to define the logical address space of a process

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Hardware Address Protection

CPU must check (at runtime) every memory access generated in user mode to be sure it is between base and limit for that user
The instructions to load the relocation and limit registers are privileged

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Sharing

Advantageous to allow each process access to the same copy of the program rather than have their own separate copy
Memory management must allow controlled access to shared areas of memory without compromising protection
Mechanisms used to support relocation support sharing capabilities

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Logical Organization

The main memory is organized as a linear, or one dimensional address space, consisting of a sequence of bytes, but:

Programs are written in modules
Modules can be written and compiled independently
Different degrees of protection given to modules (read only, execute only)
Sharing on a module level corresponds to the way of viewing the problem

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Physical Organization

Computer memory is organized into at least two levels:

Main memory (RAM)
Secondary storage (disk)

The flow of information between main memory and secondary memory is a major system concern
The responsibility for this flow should not be assigned to the individual programmer because:

Memory available for a program plus its data may be insufficient
Overlaying allows various modules to be assigned the same region of memory but is time consuming to the program
Programmer does not know how much space will be available

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Types of Partitioning

Fixed: Main memory is divided into a number of static partitions at system generation time. A process may be loaded into a partition of equal or greater size

Disadvantages:

A program may not fit into a partition
Program needs to be designed with the use of overlays
Main memory utilization is inefficient
Internal fragmentation:

Wasted space due to the block of data loaded being smaller than the partition

The number of partitions specified at system generation time limits the number of active processes in the system
Small jobs will not utilize partition space efficiently


Dynamic: Partitions are created dynamically, so that each process is loaded into a partition of exactly the size of that process.

Was used by IBM’s mainframe OS OS/MVT
Issues:

External Fragmentation:

Memory becomes more and more fragmented
Memory utilization declines

Compaction:

Technique for overcoming external fragmentation
OS shifts processes so that they are contiguous
Free memory is together in one block
Time consuming and wastes CPU time


Uses 3 placement algorithms:

Best-fit
First-fit
Next-fit


Simple Paging: Main memory is divided into a number of equal size frames. Each process is divided into a number of equal size pages of the same length as frames. A process is loaded by loading all of its pages into available, if not necessarily contiguous, frames.

Pages are chunks of a process
Frames are available chunks of memory
The method uses a “Page Table”

Maintained by the OS for each process
Contains the frame location for each page in the process
Processor must know how to access for the current process
Used by the processor to translate logical addresses into physical addresses
Kept in main memory

Address Translation Scheme is used to convert logical address into physical address

Address generated by the CPU is divided into:

Page number (p): used as an index into a page table which contains base address of each page in physical memory
Page Offset (d): Combined with the base address to define the physical memory address that is sent to the memory unit.



Simple Segmentation: Each process is divided into a number of segments. A process is loaded by loading all of its segments into dynamic partitions that need not be contiguous

Segments may vary in length
There is a maximum length
Addressing consists of two parts:

Segment number
An Offset

Similar to dynamic partitioning
Eliminates internal fragmentation

Exercises: 1:

Consider a simple paging system with a page size of 2,048 bytes.


What is the worst amount (in bytes) of internal fragmentation that can occur?
What is the average amount (in bytes) of internal fragmentation that can occur?


2: - Consider a simple paging system with a page size of 2048 bytes. A process P of size 31577 bytes needs to be loaded. 1. How many frames (or pages) are needed for process P? 2. What amount (in bytes) of internal fragmentation will occur?
3: - Assuming a 1 KB page size, what are the page numbers and offsets for the following address references? (provided as decimal values such as (page.offset)) 1. 1000 2. 3085

Virtual memory paging: As with simple paging, except that it is not necessary to load all of the pages of a process. Nonresident pages that are needed are brought in later automatically.
Virtual memory segmentation: As with simple segmentation, except that it is not necessary to load all of the segments of a process. Nonresident segments that are needed are brought in later automatically.

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Fragmentation

External Fragmentation:

Total memory space exists to satisfy a request, but is not contiguous

Internal Fragmentation:

Allocated memory may be slightly larger than requested memory; this size difference is memory internal to a partition, but not being used

First fit analysis reveals that given N blocks of allocated memory, 0.5 N blocks will be lost to fragmentation.

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Buddy System

Comprised of fixed and dynamic partitioning schemes
Space available for allocation is treated as a single block
Memory blocks are available in size 2^k words, L <= k <= U where:

2^L = smallest block that is allocated
2^U = largest block that is allocated; usually, 2^U is the size of the entire memory available for allocation

Requested block sizes are rounded up to the nearest power of 2

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Virtual Memory

Virtual memory is the separation of user logic memory from physical memory.
Importance:

Only part of the program needs to be in memory for execution
Logical address space can therefore be much larger than physical memory
Allows more efficient process creation
Less I/O needed to load or swap processes
More programs can be running concurrently

Virtual Memory Address Spaces:

Usually starts at address 0, contiguous addresses until the end of available space
Meanwhile physical memory is divided into frames
The physical page frames assigned to a process may not be contiguous
Memory management unit (MMU) maps logical to physical

Virtual memory can be implemented via:

Demand paging:

Load pages only as they are needed
If we want to run a process, we can either:

Load the entire process into memory at once
Only bring in pages as needed

This is more efficient, but complex


Demand paging is similar to paging system with swapping

Demand segmentation

Valid-Invalid Bit:

Each page table entry has a valid-invalid bit (v = in memory, i = not in memory)
Initially set to i on all entries
If the MMU encounters i during address translation, a page fault is triggered

Page Fault Handling:

Trap to the OS
Save user registers and process state
Determine the interrupt was a page fault
Check the page reference is legal; determine disk location
Issue a disk read to a free frame
Allocate CPU to another process while waiting
Receive disk I/O interrupt when complete
Restore registers and page table; resume interrupted instruction

Effective Access Time (EAT):

EAT = (1 - p) * memory access + p * (page fault overhead + swap page out + swap page in)
Where p = page fault rate (0 <= p <= 1)

Copy-on-Write (COW):

Allows parent and child processes to initially share the same pages in memory
If either process modifies a shared page, only then is the page copied
Allows more efficient process creation since only modified pages are copied

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Page Replacement Algorithms

When no free frame is available, the OS must replace a page
Goal: minimize the number of page faults
FIFO (First-In, First-Out):

Replace the oldest page in memory
Simple to implement
Suffers from Belady’s Anomaly: adding more frames can sometimes cause more page faults, not fewer

Optimal Algorithm (OPT):

Replace the page that will not be used for the longest period of time in the future
Guarantees the minimum number of page faults
Cannot be implemented in practice (requires future knowledge)
Used as a benchmark to evaluate other algorithms

Least Recently Used (LRU):

Replace the page that has not been used for the longest time in the past
Uses past knowledge as an approximation of future behavior
Generally a good algorithm; does not suffer from Belady’s Anomaly
More complex to implement than FIFO

Counting Algorithms (less common):

Least Frequently Used (LFU): replace page with smallest reference count
Most Frequently Used (MFU): replace page with largest reference count (reasoning: smallest count was likely just brought in)

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Thrashing

If a process does not have enough frames, the page-fault rate becomes very high
The process spends more time paging than executing
Leads to very low CPU utilization
OS may respond by increasing multiprogramming, making the problem worse
Occurs when: total size of localities > total memory size

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Secondary Storage

Hard Disk Drives:

Platters range from .86” to 14” (historically)
3.5”, 2.5” and 1.8” are the most common sizes
Range from 30GB to 12TB, and growing
Transfer rates reach theoretical rates of 6 Gb/sec, but are more realistically around 1 Gb/s
Seek time ranges from 3ms to 12ms, where 9ms is common on desktop drives
Latency is the time it takes for the disk to spin
Average latency = 1/2 the time it takes for a full rotation
HDDs spin platters of magnetic material at high speeds under a read-write head
Transfer rate is the rate at which data flows between the disk and a computer
Positioning/Access time is the time taken to move the disk arm to the desired cylinder (seek) and time for the desired sector to rotate under the disk head (rotational latency)
Head crash results when the read-write head touches the platter

This is really bad

Disk Performance Parameters:

The actual details of disk I/O operation depend on:

Computer System (hardware)
Operating System
Nature of the I/O channel and disk controller

On a moveable-head system, the time it takes to position the head at the track is known as seek time
The time it takes for the beginning of the sector to reach the head is known as rotational delay, or latency
The sum of the seek time and the rotational delay is known as the access time

Seek time:

The time required to move the disk arm to the required track
Three key components of seek time:

Startup time: The time it takes to accelerate the arm to its maximum speed
Settling time: The time after positioning the head over the target track until track identification is confirmed

Typical seek time is under 10ms

Rotational Delay:

The time required for the addressed area of the disk to rotate into a position where it is accessible by the read-write head
Disk rotates at speeds ranging from 3600 to 15000 RPM

Transfer time:

The transfer time to or from the disk depends on the disk rotation speed

Performance:

Average access time is the sum of the average seek time and latency

For fast disks, 3ms + 2ms = 5ms
For slow disks, 9ms + ~5.56ms = 14.56ms


Example:

To transfer a 4KB block of data on a 7200 RPM disk with a 5ms average seek time, 1 Gb/sec transfer rate with a .1ms controller overhead:

5ms + 4.17ms + transfer time =
Transfer time = 4 KB / 1 Gb/sec * 8Gb/GB * 1 GB / 1024^2KB = 32/(1024^2) = 0.00003051758 s or .031 ms
Average I/O time for 4KB block = 9.27ms + .031ms = 9.301ms


Other Nonvolatile Memory:

If disk-drive like, then called solid-state disks (SSD)
Other forms include USB drives (thumb drives, flash drives), DRAM disk replacements, surface mounted motherboards, and main storage in devices like smartphones and tablets
Can be more reliable than HDDs
More expensive per GB
Generally less capacity, but much faster
No moving parts, so no seek time or rotational latency

HDD Scheduling:

The OS is responsible for using hardware efficiently — for disk drives, this means having a fast access time and disk bandwidth

Minimize seek time

seek time ~= seek distance


Disk Bandwidth is the total number of bytes transferred, divided by the total time between the first request for service and the completion of the last transfer
We can improve both the access time and the bandwidth by managing the order in which storage I/O requests are serviced
There are many sources of disk I/O requests:

User processes
System processes
OS

I/O request includes mode, disk address, memory address, and number of sectors to transfer
OS maintains a queue of requests
Idle disk can immediately work on I/O request, but busy disk means work must queue

This means we must use optimization algorithms to determine the order in which to service requests

In the past, the OS was responsible for queue management and disk drive head scheduling, but now it is usually built into the storage devices or controllers.


Hard Drive Algorithms:

Queue of requests: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67
Assume the disk head is at 53
The disk is divided into 200 cylinders, numbered 0-199
FCFS (FIFO):

First Come First Serve
The requests are serviced in the order they arrive
Measure the total distance traveled by the disk head as a check of efficiency

SCAN:

The disk arm starts at one end of the disk and moves toward the other end, servicing requests until it reaches the other end, then reverses direction and services requests on the way back
Also called the elevator algorithm

C-SCAN:

Provides a more uniform wait time than SCAN
The head moves from one end of the disk to the other, servicing requests as it goes.

When it reaches the end, it immediately returns to the beginning of the disk, without servicing any requests on the return trip

Treats the cylinders as a circular list that wraps around from the last cylinder to the first one.

N-Step-SCAN:

Segments the disk request queue into subqueues of length N
Subqueues are processed one at a time, using SCAN
While a queue is being processed, new requests must be added to some other queue
If fewer than N requests are available at the end of the scan, all of them are processed with the next scan

FSCAN:

Uses two subqueues
When a scan begins, all of the requests are in one of the queues, with the other empty
During SCAN, all new requests are put into the other queue
Service of new requests is deferred until all of the old requests have been processed

Shortest Service Time First (SSTF):

Select the disk I/O request that requires the least movement of the disk arm from its current position
Always choose the minimum seek time
Common and has natural appeal, but can cause starvation
SCAN and C-SCAN perform better for systems under heavy disk load and have less starvation

Choosing an Algorithm:

SSTF is common and has a natural appeal with good performance
SCAN and C-SCAN perform better for systems that place a heavy load on the disk

Generally less starvation

To avoid starvation, Linux implements deadline scheduler

Maintains separate read and write queues, gives read priority
Because processes more likely to block on read than write


Track: A circular path on disk where data is recorded, structured like rings on a tree, where tracks are labeled starting from 0 on the outside and increasing as you move toward the center of the disk
Cylinder: A stack of tracks
Sector: A portion of a track, usually 512 bytes, but modern disks can have larger sectors, such as 4KB. These are grouped into blocks

Average Latency Computation:

Average latency = 1/2 * (1/RPM) * 60 seconds/minute

For a 7200 RPM disk: average latency = 1/2 * (1/7200) * 60 = 4.17ms


Equations to consider:

Rotational Latency = (60,000ms / x RPM)
Average Rotational Latency = 1/2 * Rotational Latency
Transfer Time (ms) = (Block Size (GB)) / (Transfer Rate (GB/s)) * (8Gb/s / 1 GB/s) * (1000ms / 1s) = Rotational Latency / # of sectors
Total Transfer Time = Avg Seek + Controller Overhead + Transfer Time
Average Access Time = Average Seek Time + Average Rotational Latency + Average Transfer Time
Average I/O time = Average Access Time + (amount to transfer / transfer rate) + controller overhead
Transfer rate (bytes/ms) = total track size (bytes) / one disk rev (ms)
Total Capacity of cylinder = # of platters * # of platter sides used * total capacity of a track
Total capacity of a track = capacity of cylinder * number of cylinders
Total capacity of a track = (sector size) * (sectors/track)
Time to transfer x amount of data = (x bytes) / (transfer rate in bytes/ms)
Avg time to locate and transfer a single sector (ms) = (avg seek time) + (avg rotational latency) + (1/RPM/60000)
Avg time to transfer x random sectors (ms) = (x # of sectors) * (avg time to locate and transfer a single sector)
Avg time to transfer x consecutive sectors (ms) = Average seek time + avg rotational latency + (x * sector size) / (transfer rate in bytes/ms) + controller overhead

Exercises:

Consider a disk queue holding requests to the following cylinders in the listed order: 110, 22, 3, 11, 75, 180, 100, 85, 60, 23 What is the order that the requests are serviced, assuming the disk head is at cylinder 90 and moving upward through the cylinders, using:
The FCFS scheduling algorithm
The SCAN scheduling algorithm
The C-SCAN scheduling algorithm
The SSTF scheduling algorithm
Consider a disk with 10,000 RPM, an average seek time of 8ms, and 500 sectors per track:
What is the average time to read a random sector from the disk?
What is the average time to read 100 consecutive sectors from the disk?

title: 01 · OS Overview
text:
The computer system can be divided into four main parts:

Hardware: Provide basic computing resources, and does basic calculation at request
Operating System: Controls and coordinates use of hardware among various applications and users
Application Programs: Defines ways in which the system resources are used to solve computing problems of the user

Examples: word processors, compilers, browsers, database systems and so on

Users: Humans, machines, or other computers, that can control another computer

What is a system?

A complex unit formed of many, often diverse, parts subject to a common plan, or serving a common purpose

What is an Operating System?

A complex program that acts an intermediary, or interface, between users and hardware
An OS turns awful hardware interfaces into clean, and clear abstractions for programs and users

Goals:

Executing user programs and making solving user problems easier
Making a computer convenient to use
Use hardware efficiently

Roles an OS plays:

Referee: Manages shared resources (and makes sure they’re used appropriately)

Shared Resources: Memory, CPU, disk, networks

Illusionist: Every running program (process) has infinite memory and exclusive access to the CPU
Glue: Offers a set of common services/applications independent of hardware on a system
